The F-measure is one of several external indices, including purity, precision, recall, and similarity-oriented measures like the Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient, used to evaluate clustering performance against external ground truth.

A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram used to display the results of hierarchical clustering. It visualizes both the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which clusters were merged (in an agglomerative view) or split (in a divisive view). In the diagram, the vertical height at which two clusters are joined reflects the distance between those clusters; for example, if the distance between two points is 0.11, they are joined at a height of 0.11. The root of the dendrogram is at level 1, and the diagram can be used to extract a flat clustering of K clusters by taking the clusters at the K-th level. When drawing a dendrogram by hand, the exact horizontal spacing of the leaves does not matter, but the vertical merge heights and the nested structure are essential. The leaf order must match the nested structure exactly, although branches can be flipped left-to-right. The dendrogram is distinct from the linkage criteria (such as single link, complete link, or group average) that determine the distances used to build the hierarchy.

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that starts with every object as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until one large cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is a collection of closely related clustering techniques that produce a hierarchical clustering; some have a natural interpretation in terms of graph-based clustering, while others have an interpretation in terms of a prototype-based approach. The process is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward, whereas agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward. A key component of this method is the linkage criterion, which determines how the distance between two clusters is calculated. For example, single linkage defines the distance between two clusters as the minimum distance between any two points in the clusters, expressed as d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y), where C_i and C_j are the two clusters and d(x, y) is the distance between points x and y. Other linkage methods include complete linkage (farthest pair), average linkage (all cross-pairs), centroid linkage (centers), and Ward's method, which is described as greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective. The choice of linkage method is critical because using only one approach can lead to mistakes in merging clusters; for instance, using closeness (single link) might merge clusters that almost touch instead of clusters that are intuitively more similar based on connection strength. Agglomerative clustering is often selected for global clustering tasks because it can be applied to summary information stored in clustering features. However, it has limitations: if the data is very large, it may not be directly applicable, and it can compound errors if objects are wrongly put together in a prior partitioning step, as it can never separate objects that have been merged.

Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism. Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available. Specific divisive techniques include the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering. Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, though it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory. In such large-scale scenarios, techniques such as BIRCH, which do not require that all data be in main memory, become more useful. The choice of algorithm often depends on data size and memory constraints, with divisive methods like MST serving as the divisive analog to single link agglomerative clustering.

MIN (Single Linkage) is a linkage criterion used in hierarchical clustering to define the proximity between two clusters. The proximity is defined as the minimum of the distance (or the maximum of the similarity) between any two points located in the two different clusters. Formally, the distance between two clusters Ci and Cj is calculated as dsingle(Ci, Cj) = min d(x, y), where the minimum is taken over all pairs of points x in Ci and y in Cj. In this formula, d(x, y) represents the distance between individual points x and y. Conceptually, single linkage treats two clusters as close if at least one point in one cluster is close to at least one point in the other cluster, often described as using the 'nearest bridge' between the groups. Using graph terminology, the process can be viewed as starting with all points as singleton clusters and adding links between points one at a time, shortest links first, which combines the points into clusters. In terms of implementation, single linkage allows for the use of a precomputed distance matrix; the original point-distance matrix is computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using the minimum value. The technique is noted for being good at handling non-elliptical shapes, but it is sensitive to noise and outliers.

MAX (Complete Linkage) is a version of hierarchical clustering in which the proximity of two clusters is defined as the maximum of the distance (or the minimum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters. In graph terminology, if one starts with all points as singleton clusters and adds links between points one at a time, shortest links first, a group of points is not considered a cluster until all the points in it are completely linked, i.e., form a clique. Complete linkage says two clusters are close only if even the farthest cross-cluster pair is not too far. This contrasts with single linkage, which uses the nearest bridge, and average linkage, which averages every cross-pair distance. Complete link is less susceptible to noise and outliers, but it can break large clusters and it favors globular shapes. For single and complete linkage, the original point-distance matrix is computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using min or max. For example, the complete linkage distance between clusters {A, B} and C is calculated as the maximum of the individual distances, such as max(2, 1) = 2. Similarly, the distance between {A, B, C, D} and E is the maximum of their pairwise distances, such as max(4, 3, 2, 1) = 4. Another example shows dist({3,6}, {2,5}) = max(dist(3,2), dist(6,2), dist(3,5), dist(6,5)) = max(0.15, 0.25, 0.28, 0.39) = 0.39.

Group Average Linkage is a graph-based agglomerative clustering technique that defines the proximity between two clusters as the average of the pairwise proximities (or average length of edges) of all pairs of points from different clusters. This approach bases its notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters, such as the pairwise similarity of points, rather than relying solely on the closeness of the clusters measured by the minimum distance between points. In a full agglomerative clustering run, the distance between two specified clusters is calculated as one candidate distance, which must be compared with all other current cluster-pair distances before choosing a merge. The weighted version of group average, known as WPGMA, uses coefficients that are constants independent of cluster sizes, specifically alpha_A = 1/2, alpha_B = 1/2, beta = 0, and gamma = 0. General unweighted approaches are preferred unless there is reason to believe that individual points should have different weights. For clustering approaches like group average, outliers are potentially less problematic because they tend to form singleton or small clusters that do not merge with other clusters until much later in the merging process, allowing them to be removed by discarding these small clusters.

Ward's method is a greedy bottom-up hierarchical clustering technique that uses the same objective function as K-means clustering: minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE). In this approach, each cluster is represented by its centroid, and the proximity between two clusters is defined as the increase in the total SSE that results from merging them. The algorithm builds a hierarchy by repeatedly evaluating all possible merges, computing the new total SSE for each candidate, and selecting the merge that causes the smallest increase in SSE. The SSE for a cluster C is calculated as the sum of the squared distances of its points from the cluster centroid μ_C: SSE(C) = Σ ||x - μ_C||². The total SSE is the sum of the SSEs of all clusters: SSE_total = SSE(C₁) + SSE(C₂) + ... + SSE(C_k). Ward's method is distinct from centroid linkage, which compares center-to-center distances, and from other linkage methods like single, complete, or average linkage. It is often used as a robust method for initializing K-means clustering, as it connects a local 'minimize squared error' objective to a global one. Outliers pose a serious problem for Ward's method because they increase SSE and distort centroids, unlike in single or complete linkage where outliers may form stable singleton clusters. Mathematically, Ward's method is very similar to the group average method when the proximity between two points is defined as the square of the distance between them.

Hierarchical clustering complexity refers to the computational and storage requirements of agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms, which are defined by their use of a proximity matrix and iterative cluster merging. The space complexity is O(m²), where m is the number of data points, because the algorithm must store the proximities between all pairs of points (assuming a symmetric matrix) and track the state of the clusters. The time complexity is O(m² log m) when using a sorted list or heap to optimize the search for the two closest clusters; without such optimization, the time complexity is O(m³). These high complexity requirements severely limit the size of data sets that can be processed directly, making the algorithm impractical for large-scale applications. The complexity arises from the need to perform m-1 iterations, where each iteration involves finding the closest clusters and updating the proximity matrix. While hierarchical clustering avoids the difficulty of solving hard combinatorial optimization problems and does not require choosing initial points, its computational cost is a significant drawback compared to scalable alternatives like bisecting K-means.

K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that directly divides data into K clusters, where K is a user-specified parameter representing the desired number of clusters. Each cluster is represented by a centroid, which is the representative centre of the cluster. For Euclidean K-Means, the centroid is defined as the mean of all points in the cluster; specifically, if a cluster C_i contains m_i points, the centroid c_i is calculated as the sum of the points in C_i divided by m_i. A centroid is a mean position and does not have to be one of the original data points.

The algorithm operates through an iterative procedure. First, K initial centroids are chosen. Next, each point is assigned to the closest centroid, forming the clusters. Then, each centroid is recomputed as the mean of the points assigned to it. This cycle of assignment and centroid update is repeated until the assignments stop changing or the centroids remain the same.

K-Means is a centroid-based algorithm, and its performance is often evaluated using centroid-based cohesion and separation measures. The algorithm is simple but can be sensitive to initialization; random initialization is often used, which may result in a clustering that represents a local minimum in terms of the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). While there are choices for the proximity function, centroid, and objective function that guarantee convergence, the basic algorithm's efficiency can be impacted when K is large, as the distance of each point to each cluster centroid must be calculated at each iteration.

The SSE Optimization Criterion is an objective function used in clustering that seeks to minimize the total squared error (SSE). When applied to clustering, this criterion frames the task as an optimization problem where the goal is to find a partition of points that minimizes the total SSE. Because the general clustering problem for this objective is computationally infeasible to solve exhaustively, practical algorithms use local optimization strategies. For instance, agglomerative hierarchical clustering uses the criterion to make local decisions about which clusters to merge at each step, avoiding the need to solve the hard global combinatorial optimization problem. In Ward’s method, the “minimize squared error” criterion guides the merging of clusters, although the resulting clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE and may not be stable. This local optimization approach is often used to initialize K-means clustering, indicating a connection between local and global “minimize squared error” objectives. The criterion distinguishes between global minima, which represent the best possible clustering, and local minima, which are suboptimal solutions that satisfy the objective function only within a limited region of the solution space.

K-Means Complexity refers to the computational resource requirements of the K-means clustering algorithm, specifically its time and space complexity. The space requirements for K-means are modest because the algorithm stores only the data points and centroids. The storage required is O((m+K)n), where m is the number of data points, K is the number of clusters, and n is the number of attributes. The time requirements for K-means are also modest and are basically linear in the number of data points. The time required is O(I×K×m×n), where I is the number of iterations required for convergence. Consequently, K-means is linear in m, the number of points, and is considered efficient and simple provided that K, the number of clusters, is significantly less than m. The algorithm's complexity is analyzed by considering each step of the basic K-means algorithm in detail. While the evidence notes that K-means has a time complexity, it does not provide a specific value for comparison with DBSCAN, nor does it provide the specific time and space complexity values for fuzzy c-means to allow for a direct comparison.

Centroid Initialization Sensitivity describes the dependence of K-means clustering results on the selection of initial centroids. Standard K-means is susceptible to initialization problems, which can be mitigated by using variants like bisecting K-means or by applying postprocessing to fix the resulting clusters. Bisecting K-means is less susceptible to these issues because it performs several trial bisections and selects the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), and because it operates with only two centroids at each step. An alternative initialization strategy involves selecting the first point at random or as the centroid of all points, then iteratively selecting the point farthest from any already-selected initial centroid. This approach guarantees well-separated centroids but can select outliers rather than points in dense regions, potentially leading to clusters with only one point. To address this, the farthest-point approach is often applied to a sample of points, as outliers are rare and less likely to appear in a random sample, while points from dense regions are likely to be included. K-means++ is another approach that picks centroids incrementally; at each step, each point has a probability of being picked as the new centroid proportional to the square of its distance to its closest centroid. This method is guaranteed to find a solution optimal to within a factor of O(log(k)), translating to noticeably better clustering results in terms of lower SSE. In a specific example, bisecting K-means was executed with K=3 leaf clusters using Euclidean distance, assigning objects to clusters, computing SSE, and finding centroids in each iteration, with initial centroids p10 and p11.

K-Means and its variations have specific limitations regarding the types of clusters they can detect. The algorithm requires a meaningful distance metric and a meaningful mean; consequently, it cannot be applied to raw categories because such data do not have meaningful averages. Traditional K-Means is sensitive to outliers and has difficulty handling clusters that differ significantly in size or density, or that possess non-globular shapes. When clusters have non-spherical shapes or widely different sizes or densities, K-Means struggles to identify the natural groupings. For instance, if one cluster is much larger than others, the larger cluster may be broken while a smaller cluster is combined with a portion of the larger one. Similarly, if smaller clusters are much denser than a larger cluster, the algorithm fails to find the natural clusters. In cases where the natural clusters are not globular, K-Means may produce clusters that mix portions of the natural groups. Additionally, the algorithm is subject to convergence issues where it reaches a local minimum, meaning it cannot improve from its current path, rather than finding the global minimum where no possible clustering with the same K has a lower total SSE.

Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by constructing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits. Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points. The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2. This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. A key characteristic of this approach is that it performs several trial bisections for each split and retains the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), which makes it less susceptible to initialization problems compared to standard K-Means. Additionally, because each split only requires computing distances to two centroids for a subset of points, Bisecting K-Means can run significantly faster than regular K-Means, particularly when the number of clusters is large. The algorithm produces a hierarchical structure; if a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from the bisecting process can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step. However, if the goal is to preserve the hierarchical structure, the process stops after the final split.

A distance function d(x, y) between two points x and y is characterized by three fundamental properties: positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Positivity requires that d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y, and that d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y. Symmetry requires that d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y. The triangle inequality requires that d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points x, y, and z. These properties define the standard behavior of distances such as the Euclidean distance. A dissimilarity measure that fails to satisfy these properties, such as a set-based distance defined as the size of the set difference A - B, can be modified to satisfy them by using the sum of the sizes of both set differences, size(A - B) + size(B - A).

A similarity function s(x, y) quantifies the similarity between two points x and y. The typical properties of a similarity function include symmetry and positivity, whereas the triangle inequality (or an analogous property) typically does not hold for similarities. A specific property stated for similarity functions is that s(x, y) = 1 only if x = y, with the constraint that 0 ≤ s ≤ 1. In the context of interval or ratio attributes, similarity is typically expressed by transforming a dissimilarity into a similarity. The evidence also notes that dissimilarity measures can be modified to satisfy specific properties, such as using d(A, B) = size(A-B) + size(B-A) to ensure properties hold for set-based dissimilarities, though this specific modification is framed in the context of dissimilarity measures rather than similarity functions directly.

Euclidean distance is a metric distance measure used to quantify the proximity between two points in Euclidean space. It is a specific case of the Lp norm distance family and is the most commonly used proximity measure in the literature for dense, continuous data. The measure is defined by the formula d(x, y) = √((x₁ - y₁)² + (x₂ - y₂)²), where x and y are the coordinates of the two points being compared. As a distance function, Euclidean distance satisfies the standard metric properties: positivity (d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y), identity of indiscernibles (d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y), symmetry (d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y), and the triangle inequality (d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points x, y, and z). In practice, Euclidean distance is frequently employed in clustering algorithms such as K-means, where it serves as the basis for calculating the sum of squared errors (SSE) to evaluate cluster quality. It is also used in imputation methods like K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) to identify the closest instances for estimating missing values. While Euclidean distance compares the absolute locations of points, it is distinct from similarity measures like cosine similarity, which compares direction or pattern, and from other distance metrics like Manhattan distance, which measures distance by moving step-by-step along the axes.

Manhattan distance is a distance measure that quantifies the separation between two points by summing the absolute differences of their coordinates, effectively measuring the distance if one moves step by step along the axes, like walking through city blocks. Formally, for two points x and y with m dimensions, the Manhattan distance is defined as d_Manhattan(x, y) = Σ_{i=1}^{m} |x_i - y_i|. This measure is bounded such that 0 ≤ d_Manhattan(x, y) < ∞. In the context of clustering, when the objective is to minimize the sum of the distances, the appropriate centroid for a cluster using Manhattan distance is the median of the points in that cluster. This distinguishes it from similarity scores, where larger values indicate greater similarity, and from Euclidean distance, which is calculated using the square root of the sum of squared differences.

Cosine similarity is a similarity score used to measure the relationship between two data objects, such as documents represented as vectors. Unlike distance measures such as Manhattan or Euclidean distance, which quantify how far apart two points are, cosine similarity quantifies how similar two objects are, with larger values indicating greater similarity. It is defined as the cosine of the angle between the two vectors. When the cosine similarity is 1, the angle between the vectors is 0 degrees, meaning they point in the same direction and are identical except for length. When the cosine similarity is 0, the angle is 90 degrees, indicating the vectors are perpendicular and do not share any terms. When the cosine similarity is -1, the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.

The calculation involves normalizing the vectors by dividing each by its length, resulting in unit vectors. For unit vectors, the cosine similarity can be calculated as a simple inner product. This normalization means that cosine similarity does not take the length of the data objects into account, making it particularly useful for sparse data such as documents where the magnitude of the vector (e.g., document length) may not be relevant to the similarity of content. In contrast, Euclidean distance compares locations and is sensitive to length, making it more appropriate for dense data or when magnitude is important. Cosine similarity is often used in clustering algorithms, such as K-means variants, to maximize the cohesion of clusters by maximizing the similarity of objects to the cluster centroid.

The Rand Index is an external validation measure used to evaluate clustering by comparing the cluster structure against true class labels. It is a similarity-oriented measure that operates by comparing pairs of distinct objects, meaning it does not require the original feature values once cluster assignments and class labels are available. The index is calculated using the formula: Rand Index = (f11 + f00) / (f11 + f10 + f01 + f00). In this formula, f11 represents pairs of objects that are in the same cluster and belong to the same class, while f00 represents pairs that are in different clusters and belong to different classes. The denominator represents the total number of pairs of distinct objects. The Rand Index specifically includes f00, the pairs that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering. This distinguishes it from the Jaccard Coefficient, which ignores f00 and focuses only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. Because the Rand Index includes f00, it is often higher than the Jaccard Coefficient. The measure can be computed through class similarity and cluster similarity matrices, where diagonal elements (representing objects compared to themselves) are not counted because only pairs of distinct objects are considered. In some contexts, the adjusted Rand index is used, which is based on the multivariate hypergeometric distribution to allow for the computation of p-values.

The Jaccard coefficient is a similarity measure used to quantify the similarity between two binary vectors, particularly in contexts involving asymmetric binary attributes such as transaction data where a value of 1 indicates the presence of an item and 0 indicates its absence. It is frequently employed as a cluster validity measure and is often symbolized by j. The coefficient is defined by the formula Jaccard coefficient = f11 / (f11 + f10 + f01), where f11 represents the number of attributes where both objects have a 1, f10 represents the number of attributes where the first object has a 1 and the second has a 0, and f01 represents the number of attributes where the first object has a 0 and the second has a 1. A key characteristic of this measure is that it ignores f00, the count of attributes where both objects have a 0, focusing exclusively on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. This distinguishes it from other similarity measures like the Simple Matching Coefficient (Rand statistic), which includes f00 in its calculation. For example, given f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Jaccard coefficient is calculated as 2 / (2 + 2 + 2) = 0.33. The measure can also be extended to more than two variables using multidimensional contingency tables, and an extended version exists for document data that reduces to the standard Jaccard coefficient for binary attributes.

A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set. The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity. Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity. To facilitate comparison, similarity values are frequently transformed to this standard range using a linear transformation such as s' = (s - min_s) / (max_s - min_s), where s is the original similarity value, and min_s and max_s are the minimum and maximum similarity values in the data set. This transformation preserves the relative distances between points.

In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix. An ideal cluster similarity matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the associated pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise. When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, this ideal matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere. The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known as Hubert's Γ statistic.

The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results. By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships between clusters. For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks. Additionally, in centroid-based clustering, the pairwise similarity or distance of the centroids can be computed to provide a more comprehensive view of cluster cohesion and separation. This approach is analogous to examining a confusion matrix in classification problems rather than relying solely on aggregate measures like accuracy or the F-measure.

A missing value occurs when a data object lacks one or more attribute values, or when entire data objects are absent from a dataset. This condition can arise because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are a data quality issue that must be addressed during data analysis, as they can affect the reliability of the analysis if many objects are affected. Different machine learning models handle missing values in distinct ways. For example, Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values in the training set by ignoring the missing values of every attribute while computing conditional probability estimates, and handle missing values in test instances by using only the non-missing attribute values to compute posterior probabilities. However, this approach is inaccurate if the frequency of missing values for a particular attribute value depends on the class label. Bayesian networks can also handle missing values during training and testing by treating the missing attribute as an unobserved node and marginalizing out its effect on the target class. In contrast, logistic regression cannot handle data instances with missing values because it computes posterior probabilities by taking a weighted sum of all attributes; if a test instance has missing values, logistic regression fails to predict its class label. Similarly, artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle instances with missing values in either the training or testing phase. Decision tree classifiers offer several specific strategies for handling missing values in test sets. The probabilistic split method, used by the C4.5 classifier, distributes the data instance to every child of the splitting node according to the probability that the missing attribute has a particular value. The surrogate split method, used by the CART algorithm, assigns the instance to one of the child nodes based on the value of another non-missing surrogate attribute whose splits most resemble the partitions made by the missing attribute. The separate class method, used by the CHAID algorithm, treats the missing value as a separate categorical value distinct from other values of the splitting attribute. Other strategies for dealing with missing values are based on data preprocessing, where the instance with a missing value is either imputed with the mode (for categorical attributes) or mean (for continuous attributes) value, or discarded before the classifier is trained. A simple and effective strategy is to eliminate objects with missing values, which may be expedient if only a few objects are affected, but can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible if many objects have missing values. A related strategy is to eliminate attributes that have missing values, but this should be done with caution because the eliminated attributes may be critical to the analysis. Sometimes missing data can be reliably estimated. For example, in a time series that changes in a reasonably smooth fashion, missing values can be estimated (interpolated) by using the remaining values. In a dataset with many similar data points, the attribute values of the points closest to the point with the missing value are often used to estimate the missing value; for continuous attributes, the average attribute value of the nearest neighbors is used, and for categorical attributes, the most commonly occurring attribute value can be taken. For instance, precipitation measurements for areas not containing a ground station can be estimated using values observed at nearby ground stations. In clustering, if one or both objects of a pair have missing values for some attributes, the similarity can be calculated by using only the attributes that do not have missing values, though the similarity will only be approximate. There is no universal imputation method which performs best for all classifiers.

A missingness mechanism describes the underlying process that determines which values in a dataset are missing. Categorizing these mechanisms is a critical step in data preprocessing because the assumptions made about the missingness mechanism and the pattern of missing values directly affect which treatment methods can be correctly applied. The evidence specifically defines the Missing at Random (MAR) mechanism, which is a specific type of missingness mechanism. In the MAR case, the data is partitioned into an observed part (Xobs) and a missing part (Xmis). The defining property of MAR is that the probability of an observation being missing may depend on the observed data (Xobs) but does not depend on the missing data (Xmis). Formally, this is expressed by the condition that the distribution of the missingness indicator B, given the full data X and parameters ζ, is independent of Xmis: P(B|Xobs, Xmis, ζ) = P(B|Xobs, ζ). This implies that for a given set of observed features, the distribution of the remaining features is the same among observed cases as it is among missing cases. The choice of missingness mechanism is also a prerequisite for specific treatments; for instance, multiple imputation (MI) is only applicable when the data follows a Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) or MAR mechanism. Simple preprocessing operations often ignore the missingness mechanism entirely, whereas advanced methods require this categorization to function correctly.

The Deletion Strategy is a data preprocessing approach used to handle missing values by removing incomplete records or features from a dataset. The primary method involves eliminating data objects (rows) that contain missing values. This approach is considered simple and effective, particularly when only a small number of objects have missing data, as it may be expedient to omit them. However, this strategy carries risks: even partially specified objects contain information, and if many objects have missing values, reliable analysis can become difficult or impossible. A related variant of the deletion strategy is the elimination of attributes (columns) that have missing values. This should be done with caution, as the eliminated attributes may be critical to the analysis. The strategy is distinct from imputation, which involves estimating missing values rather than removing the data.

Imputation is the process of replacing missing values (MVs) in a dataset with estimated values. It is distinguished from deletion strategies, which remove cases or attributes, and from the classification of missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, NMAR), which describe how data is lost. The goal of imputation is to obtain values for non-reference attributes (attributes with missing data) for incomplete objects, using the available reference attributes. 

Imputation methods can be broadly categorized into statistical and machine learning approaches. Statistical methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Imputation, model the underlying probability distribution of the data. For example, in a simple binomial case where the probability of heads is θ, the maximum likelihood estimate is derived as θ̂ = h/n, where h is the number of heads and n is the total number of flips. More formally, the likelihood is obtained from a binomial distribution: P(θ) = C(n,h) * θ^h * (1-θ)^(n-h). The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is another statistical approach that assumes the data follows a probability distribution, such as a multivariate Gaussian, and iteratively revises estimates of the mean and covariance to impute missing values using conditional expectations.

Machine learning-based imputation methods, such as K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI) and Fuzzy K-means Clustering Imputation, do not require assuming a specific underlying distribution. KMI divides the dataset into K clusters and uses the cluster centroids to impute missing values. The algorithm involves three processes: (1) randomly selecting K complete data objects as centroids, (2) iteratively modifying the partition to reduce the sum of distances between objects and their cluster centroids until a threshold is met, and (3) filling in non-reference attributes for incomplete objects based on the cluster information. In Fuzzy K-means, each data object belongs to all K clusters with different membership degrees, and the imputed value for a non-reference attribute j is calculated as the sum of the membership degree of the object in each cluster multiplied by the centroid value for that attribute: x_{i,j} = Σ_{k=1}^{K} U(x_i, ν_k) * ν_{k,j}. 

The choice of imputation method depends on the context. In unsupervised settings, methods that generate values close to the true unknown values are preferred, often evaluated using Mean Square Error (MSE) or Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). In supervised settings, such as classification, a good imputation method enables the classifier to obtain better accuracy, which is harder to measure directly. The use of machine learning methods for imputation alleviates the need to search for the estimated underlying distribution of the data, but they are still subject to the MAR (Missing At Random) assumption to be correctly applied.

Data integration is the process of merging data elements from different sources into a single, unified data set. This step is necessary when data originates from multiple or heterogeneous sources, as gathering these elements together is a complex task. A core challenge in data integration is matching schemas from different sources, which often leads to issues such as inconsistent and duplicated tuples, as well as redundant and correlated attributes. Different attribute names or table schemes can produce uneven examples that require consolidation, and attribute values may represent the same concept under different names, creating inconsistencies in the resulting instances.

An essential part of the integration process is building a data map that establishes how each instance should be arranged in a common structure to represent a real-world example. When data is obtained from relational databases, it is usually flattened and gathered into a single record. While some database frameworks allow users to provide a map to traverse the database directly using in-database access utilities, extracting the data to an external file is often the preferred option for preprocessing. Keeping data in the database requires preprocessing to be applied repeatedly, whereas extracting it to an external file allows for faster processing and modeling if the data is preprocessed and fits in memory.

If the integration process is not performed properly, redundancies and inconsistencies will appear, resulting in a decrease in the accuracy and speed of subsequent data mining processes. Automatic approaches for data integration exist in the literature, ranging from techniques that match and find data schemas to automatic procedures that reconcile different schemas. It is important to note that even after data is correctly integrated, it may still contain errors, such as missing data, wrong data, or non-standard representations, which are typically addressed by subsequent data cleaning steps.

An attribute is considered redundant when it can be derived from another attribute or a set of other attributes, or when it is strongly correlated with another attribute in the data. Redundancy is a data quality issue that should be avoided because it increases the size of the data set, which in turn increases the modeling time of data mining algorithms and may induce overfitting in the obtained model. Inconsistencies in dimension or attribute names can also cause redundancies, particularly when data is merged from different sources where the same concept is represented by different names or where some attributes are calculated from others.

Redundancies in attributes can be detected using correlation analysis, which measures the strength of the implication of one attribute to another. For nominal data with a finite set of values, the chi-squared (χ²) test is commonly applied. The procedure involves creating a contingency table with joint events (Ai, Bj), where attribute A takes the value ai and attribute B takes the value bj. The χ² statistic is computed as the sum over all joint events of the squared difference between the observed frequency (oij) and the expected frequency (eij), divided by the expected frequency: χ² = ΣΣ (oij - eij)² / eij. The expected frequency eij is computed as (count(A = ai) × count(B = bj)) / m, where m is the number of instances in the data set, count(A = ai) is the number of instances with the value ai for attribute A, and count(B = bj) is the number of instances having the value bj for attribute B. The χ² test checks the hypothesis that A and B are independent, with (r-1)×(c-1) degrees of freedom, where c and r are the number of distinct values for attributes A and B, respectively. If the computed statistic is above the critical value from a χ² table at the established significance level, the null hypothesis of independence is rejected, indicating that A and B are statistically correlated.

For numeric attributes, the use of the correlation coefficient and the covariance is typical. The correlation coefficient rA,B is computed as the sum of the products of the deviations of the values of A and B from their respective means, divided by the product of the number of instances, the standard deviation of A, and the standard deviation of B: rA,B = Σ (ai - Ā)(bi - B̄) / (m σA σB). Here, ai and bi are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, Ā and B̄ are the mean values of A and B, and σA and σB are the standard deviations of A and B. Checking whether two numerical attributes are highly correlated is useful to determine if they are redundant.

Different machine learning models handle redundant attributes in different ways. Decision trees can handle redundant attributes because redundant attributes show similar gains in purity if they are selected for splitting, so only one of them will be selected as an attribute test condition. Logistic regression can learn equal weights for every redundant attribute that is a duplicate of another, without degrading classification performance, although a large number of redundant attributes in high-dimensional settings can make it susceptible to overfitting. Linear SVMs can handle redundant attributes by learning similar weights for the duplicate attributes, and their regularization makes them more robust to the presence of a large number of redundant attributes than other classifiers. Rule-based classifiers can handle redundant attributes because once an attribute has been used as a conjunct in a rule antecedent, the remaining redundant attributes would show little to no information gain and would thus be ignored. Bayesian networks can handle correlated or redundant attributes because they do not use the naïve Bayes assumption about conditional independence, but instead are able to express richer forms of conditional independence. In contrast, the presence of a large number of redundant attributes can adversely affect the performance of nearest neighbor classifiers by biasing proximity measures toward such attributes, resulting in improper estimates of distance. In the context of rule selection, the total description length for a class includes a tuning parameter g whose value depends on the number of redundant attributes present in the model; the value of g is small if the model contains many redundant attributes.

Duplicate tuples are repeated instances of data records that appear in a dataset, often arising from the use of denormalized tables or errors in the data entry process. These duplicates are a significant concern in data preprocessing because they waste storage space and computing time for data mining algorithms and can serve as a source of inconsistency. A particularly difficult form of duplication occurs when minor differences in attribute values, such as identifier fields, cause identical repeated instances to be treated as distinct records; these near-duplicates are harder to detect than simple exact matches. Duplicate tuples frequently emerge during the data integration process, where matching schemas from different sources can introduce redundancies and inconsistencies that degrade the accuracy and speed of subsequent data mining tasks. While data obtained from relational databases is often flattened into single records, extracting this data is generally preferred over in-database mining to facilitate proper preprocessing and the detection of such duplications.

Inconsistent values are data quality issues where recorded attribute values differ from the true values or violate established constraints. This can occur when information is sourced from different systems with varying measurement standards, leading to instances that are actually the same but not identified as such. A common manifestation is when attribute values fall outside the range established in the dataset's metadata, a condition that is relatively easy to check. A specific example is an address field where the listed zip code and city do not correspond to the same geographic area, potentially caused by digit transposition during manual entry or misreading during scanning. In the context of duplicate detection, inconsistent values must be resolved when two data objects represent a single entity but have differing attribute values. It is important to detect and, if possible, correct these problems to ensure data integrity, while being careful not to merge distinct objects that merely share similar attributes.

Data cleaning is the preprocessing step that detects and corrects data inaccuracies to remove or repair dirty data before applying data mining techniques. It is usually performed after data integration, when the data is computer-readable and constitutes a unique source, but a uniform data set without measurable inconsistencies is not necessarily clean. Dirty data typically appears as missing data or wrong (noisy) data, arising from data entry errors, data update errors, data transmission errors, or bugs in the data processing system. The goal is to filter or correct wrong data so that subsequent data mining algorithms can handle the data and extract accurate knowledge. A high proportion of dirty data in training or testing sets can produce less reliable models, with the impact depending on the algorithm: decision trees (especially higher-order trees), artificial neural networks, and distance-based algorithms like KNN are known to be susceptible to noise. Data cleaning is distinct from data normalization and transformation, which adapt the data set to the needs of the algorithm, and from removing redundant attributes, which addresses size and efficiency rather than accuracy.

Normalization and transformation are data preprocessing techniques used to adapt a dataset to the specific requirements of downstream data mining algorithms. A variable transformation is defined as a modification applied to all values of a variable, where the transformation is applied to the value of the variable for each object. For example, if only the magnitude of a variable is important, the values can be transformed by taking the absolute value.

Normalization is a specific type of transformation often used to rescale data to a common range. In the literature, normalization usually refers to a particular case of min-max normalization where the final interval is [0, 1], meaning the new minimum is 0 and the new maximum is 1. The interval [-1, 1] is also typical when normalizing data. An alternative, but equivalent, formulation for min-max normalization uses a base value (new-min_A) and a desired new range (R) in which the values will be mapped after the transformation. The formula for this transformation is: v' = new-min_A + R * ((v - min_A) / (max_A - min_A)), where v is the original value, v' is the transformed value, min_A and max_A are the original minimum and maximum attribute values, new-min_A is the base value, and R is the desired new range.

Normalization is particularly useful for learning methods based on distances, such as artificial neural networks (ANNs) or distance-based methods. Rescaling all data to the same range avoids attributes with a large range difference from dominating the distance calculation, which could mislead the learning process by giving more importance to those attributes. Normalization also helps speed up the learning process in ANNs by helping weights converge faster. In some cases, transformation or normalization is needed to obtain a proper similarity measure, such as when dealing with time series that have trends or periodic patterns.

A specific transformation useful for obtaining a new variable that behaves like a normally distributed one involves using the rank of the observation and the cumulative normal function. However, this transformation cannot be applied separately to training and test partitions; it is only recommended when the test and training data are the same. Data normalization and transformation techniques are essential because a consistent and error-free dataset is not necessarily in the best form for a data mining algorithm. Some algorithms work much better with normalized attribute values, while others may not be able to work with nominal-valued attributes or may benefit from subtle transformations in the data.

A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against the true labels of instances in a test set. It is the most basic approach for representing classification performance and provides a concise, detailed representation of how a model predicts correctly or incorrectly. For a binary classification problem, the matrix is organized with rows representing the true class and columns representing the predicted class. The four entries in the matrix are defined as follows: True Positives (TP) are instances where the actual class is positive and the predicted class is positive; False Negatives (FN) are instances where the actual class is positive but the predicted class is negative; False Positives (FP) are instances where the actual class is negative but the predicted class is positive; and True Negatives (TN) are instances where the actual class is negative and the predicted class is negative. 

The confusion matrix is used to evaluate models on test sets that are independent of the training sets, ensuring the model can accurately predict class labels for instances it has never encountered before. While the matrix provides the information needed to determine how well a classification model performs, it is often difficult to interpret and compare the performance of classifiers using the four-dimensional representations provided by the counts. Consequently, the counts in the confusion matrix are often summarized using evaluation measures, such as accuracy, which combines these four counts into a single value. Accuracy is used extensively when classes are balanced, but it is not suitable for data sets with imbalanced class distributions because it tends to favor classifiers that correctly classify the majority class. In such cases, other measures that capture different criteria of performance are used. The confusion matrix is also applicable in contexts where classes are not equally important, and it can be used to provide the most detailed information in cluster analysis, similar to its role in classification.

Accuracy is a fundamental evaluation metric used to assess the quality of classification models and rules. In the context of binary classification, it is formally defined as the ratio of correct predictions to the total number of predictions. This is expressed by the formula: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN), where TP represents true positives, TN represents true negatives, FP represents false positives, and FN represents false negatives. An equivalent general definition states that accuracy is the number of correct predictions divided by the number of all predictions. In the evaluation of specific classification rules, accuracy (also referred to as the confidence factor) is defined as the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels match the predicted class. Accuracy serves as a baseline for comparing different classification methods; however, a raw accuracy difference between two classifiers is not automatically a significant win. Statistical tests, such as a Z-statistic, are used to determine if one classifier is significantly better than another. Furthermore, measured accuracy is an estimate based on a finite test set and is subject to sampling uncertainty. Accuracy can be misleading, particularly under class imbalance, as it may hide poor performance on the positive class. In such cases, other metrics like precision and recall are often necessary to provide a more complete evaluation.

Precision is an evaluation measure for binary classification that quantifies the fraction of correct predictions of the positive class over the total number of positive predictions. It is also referred to as the positive predicted value (PPV). The standard formula for precision is p = TP / (TP + FP), where TP represents true positives and FP represents false positives. A classifier with high precision is likely to have most of its positive predictions correct, making it a useful measure for highly skewed test sets where positive predictions, even though small in numbers, are required to be mostly correct. Precision is sensitive to class skew; when selecting a score threshold for a classifier optimized for precision, the skew of the validation set should be similar to that of the test set to ensure optimal performance. In the context of statistical testing, precision is closely related to the false discovery rate (FDR), with the relationship precision = 1 - FDR. Precision captures the effect of false positives but not false negatives; a classifier that is very conservative in classifying instances as positive to reduce false positives may achieve high precision but very poor recall. A perfect classifier is characterized by precision = 1 and recall = 1.

Recall, also known as sensitivity, is a classifier evaluation metric that measures the proportion of actual positive instances correctly identified by the model. In the medical community, this metric is referred to as sensitivity, while in the information retrieval literature, it is called recall. A classifier with a high recall value has a high chance of correctly identifying the positive instances in the data. The metric is calculated using the formula: Recall = TP / (TP + FN), where TP represents true positives and FN represents false negatives. In a specific evaluation example, a classifier with 2 true positives and 1 false negative yields a recall of 2/3, or approximately 0.667 (66.7%). This value is identical to the sensitivity calculated for the same dataset, confirming that sensitivity and recall are equivalent metrics. The calculation relies on the confusion matrix components, specifically the count of true positives and false negatives, to determine the model's ability to capture all relevant positive cases.

Specificity, also known as the true negative rate (TNR), is a classifier evaluation metric defined as the fraction of negative test instances correctly predicted by the classifier. Formally, it is calculated as the number of true negatives (TN) divided by the sum of true negatives and false positives (FP), expressed as Specificity = TN / (TN + FP). In this formula, TN represents the count of actual negative cases correctly identified as negative, and FP represents the count of actual negative cases incorrectly identified as positive. Specificity checks how many actual negatives were correctly rejected, distinguishing it from precision, which checks the quality of positive predictions, and accuracy, which counts all correct predictions. It is not the same as precision for the negative class because specificity uses actual negatives in the denominator, whereas negative predictive value would use predicted negatives. In a worked example, a classifier with 5 true negatives and 2 false positives yields a specificity of 5/7, or approximately 71.4%.

The F-Measure is an evaluation measure used to evaluate a match. A related formula, denoted as F_B, is provided in the source as: F_B = (β2 + 1) r p r + β2 p = (β2 + 1) × TP (β2 + 1) TP + β3 2 FP + FN. The source also notes that the F-measure and hierarchical F-measure are examples of how to evaluate such a match.

A confidence interval for accuracy is an interval of parameter values in which an estimated accuracy value is guaranteed to fall a certain percentage of times, known as the confidence level. It is used to quantify the inherent uncertainty in a classifier's performance because accuracy measured on a finite test set is only an estimate. The interval is often reported along with point estimates to express how much the true accuracy could plausibly differ due to sampling variation.

The derivation of the confidence interval for accuracy models the classification task as a binomial random experiment. Given a test set of N instances, let X be the number of instances correctly predicted and p be the true accuracy. The empirical accuracy is defined as acc = X/N. The binomial distribution for X has a mean of Np and a variance of Np(1-p). The empirical accuracy acc has a binomial distribution with mean p and variance p(1-p)/N. When N is sufficiently large, the binomial distribution can be approximated by a normal distribution, which allows the confidence interval for acc to be derived.

The general form of the confidence interval is the estimate plus or minus an uncertainty margin. For a 90% two-sided interval, the formula uses the Z-value Z0.95 = 1.64. Larger test sets produce smaller standard errors, resulting in a narrower confidence interval. In a specific example, a model with an accuracy of 80% evaluated on 100 test instances yields a confidence interval between 71.1% and 86.7% at a 95% confidence level, where the Z-value is 1.96.

seed_body: Comparing two models on independent test sets is a statistical evaluation task used to determine whether the observed difference in performance between two classification models is statistically significant. This approach is necessary because a raw difference in accuracy or error rates may be due to random variation rather than a true difference in model quality. The setup involves two models, typically denoted as M1 and M2, which are evaluated on two distinct, independent test sets, D1 and D2. The number of instances in each test set is denoted as n1 and n2, respectively. The error rate for model M1 on test set D1 is denoted as e1, and the error rate for model M2 on test set D2 is denoted as e2. The primary goal is to test the statistical significance of the difference between e1 and e2. A key difficulty in this comparison is that the significance of the performance difference depends on the size of the test sets; for example, a model achieving 85% accuracy on a test set of 30 instances is not directly comparable in statistical confidence to a model achieving 75% accuracy on a test set of 5,000 instances. The evidence provided establishes the problem definition and the variables involved but does not specify the particular statistical test or formula used to perform the comparison.

The significance level, denoted by the Greek letter alpha (α), is a fixed constant in hypothesis testing whose value is decided before any tests are performed. It is defined as the probability of incurring a type I error, which is the probability of the critical region under the null hypothesis. In practice, a result is called statistically significant if it has a p-value lower than the pre-specified threshold α. Rejecting the null hypothesis if the test statistic falls in the critical region is equivalent to evaluating the p-value and rejecting the null hypothesis if the p-value falls below α. While every result has a different p-value, the significance level α remains a fixed constant. Common choices for the level of significance are 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%). In the context of multiple testing, such as the Bonferroni procedure, the significance level for every individual test may be adjusted (e.g., to α/m) to control the family-wise error rate (FWER). For FDR controlling procedures, α represents the desired false discovery rate and is often chosen to have a value greater than 0.05, such as 0.20. The significance level is distinct from the p-value, which is a result-specific metric, and from the critical value, which is a threshold derived from α for a specific test statistic distribution.

One-sided and two-sided tests are statistical procedures used to evaluate whether an observed result is a significant departure from a null hypothesis. The test statistic, typically a count or real-valued quantity, measures how 'extreme' an observed result is under the null hypothesis. A one-sided test focuses on a specific direction of difference, such as testing whether model A is better than model B, and is categorized as either right-tailed or left-tailed. In contrast, a two-sided test asks whether the models are different in either direction. The distinction is reflected in the distribution of the significance level (alpha) across the tails of the null distribution: a two-sided test with alpha = 0.05 allocates 0.025 probability to each tail, whereas a one-sided test places the entire 0.05 probability in a single tail. A low p-value indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution for both types of tests, providing sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. For a two-tailed test, the decision rule typically uses a threshold such as |Z| > 1.96 at alpha = 0.05, while a 90% two-sided interval uses Z0.95 = 1.64. Larger test sets produce smaller standard errors, which results in narrower confidence intervals.

The role of test sample size in model evaluation is defined by the direct dependence of measured accuracy on the specific test sample used. When selecting a sample size, there is a fundamental trade-off: larger sample sizes increase the probability that the sample will be representative of the underlying data, but they also eliminate much of the computational advantage of sampling. Conversely, smaller sample sizes carry the risk of missing true patterns or detecting erroneous ones. This impact on representativeness is demonstrated by a data set containing 8000 two-dimensional points, where a sample of 2000 points preserves most of the data structure, while a sample of 500 points misses much of it. In the context of cluster analysis, the probability of capturing all structures is highly sensitive to sample size; for a data set with 10 clusters, a sample size of 20 has only a 20% chance of including all clusters, and even a sample size of 30 has an almost 40% chance of missing objects from at least one cluster. These examples illustrate that sample size is a critical parameter that directly influences the reliability and representativeness of the evaluation results.

An ensemble classifier is a model that combines several base classifiers to make a single final prediction. The base classifiers are often individually imperfect, but their combined decision can be more robust. For classification, a common combination rule is majority voting, where the predicted class is the majority of the individual predictions: ŷ = majority{h1(x), h2(x),..., hB(x)}. An alternate approach is a weighted majority vote, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance. The ensemble of classifiers can be constructed in many ways, including by manipulating the training set. In this approach, multiple training sets are created by resampling the original data according to some sampling distribution and constructing a classifier from each training set. Bagging and boosting are two examples of ensemble methods that manipulate their training sets. The base classifiers for most of these approaches can be generated sequentially (one after another) or in parallel (all at once). Once an ensemble of classifiers has been learned, a test example is classified by combining the predictions made by the base classifiers. The ensemble classifier predicts the class label of a test example by taking a majority vote on the predictions made by the base classifiers. If the base classifiers are identical, then all the base classifiers will commit the same mistakes, and the error rate of the ensemble remains the same as the base classifiers. On the other hand, if the base classifiers are independent—i.e., their errors are uncorrelated—then the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly. The ensemble classifier performs worse than the base classifiers when the base classifier error rate is larger than 0.5. Two necessary conditions for an ensemble classifier to perform better than a single classifier are: (1) the base classifiers should be independent of each other, and (2) the base classifiers should do better than a classifier that performs random guessing. In practice, it is difficult to ensure total independence among the base classifiers, but improvements in classification accuracies have been observed in ensemble methods in which the base classifiers are somewhat correlated. Even though each base classifier is a decision stump, combining the classifiers can lead to a decision boundary that mimics a decision tree of depth 2.
